source_refs.note: Book p. 99-101: 6.5.2 Properties of G.P. (i)-(vi), Examples 12-16 (Ex 14 Step 1/Step 2); Exercise 6.5 not included

blocks.text: (i) If each term of a G.P. is multiplied or divided by the same non-zero number, then the resulting sequence is also a G.P. i.e., if \(g_1, g_2, g_3, \ldots, g_n, \ldots\) are in G.P. and \(k\) is a non-zero number, then

items: (a) \(kg_1, kg_2, kg_3, \ldots, kg_n, \ldots\) are in G.P.

blocks.text: (ii) The reciprocals of the terms of a G.P. also form a G.P. i.e., if \(a, b, c\) are in G.P., then \(\frac{1}{a}, \frac{1}{b}, \frac{1}{c}\) are also in G.P.
(iii) If each term of a G.P. be raised to the same power, the resulting numbers also form a G.P. i.e., if \(a, b, c\) are in G.P., then \(a^{n}, b^{n}, c^{n}\) are also in G.P.
(iv) Three numbers \(a, b, c\) are in G.P. if and only if \(b^{2} = ac\).
(v) If the set of positive numbers \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots, a_n, \ldots\) are in G.P., then \(\log a_1, \log a_2, \log a_3, \ldots, \log a_n, \ldots\) are also in A.P. and vice-versa.

(vi) Term by term multiplication or division of two G.Ps. are also in G.P. i.e., if \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots, a_n\) and \(b_1, b_2, b_3, \ldots, b_n\) are in G.P. then \(a_1b_1, a_2b_2, a_3b_3, \ldots\) and \(\frac{a_1}{b_1}, \frac{a_2}{b_2}, \frac{a_3}{b_3}, \ldots\) are also in G.P.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Each property can be seen on the G.P. \(2, 6, 18\) (\(r = 3\)):
(i) \(\times 5\): \(10, 30, 90\) (\(r = 3\)); \(\div 2\): \(1, 3, 9\) (\(r = 3\)).
(ii) Reciprocals: \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{6}, \frac{1}{18}\) (\(r = \frac{1}{3}\)).
(iii) Squares: \(4, 36, 324\) (\(r = 9\)).
(iv) \(6^{2} = 36 = 2 \times 18\).
(v) \(\log 2, \log 6, \log 18\): each differs from the next by \(\log 3\), so they form an A.P.
(vi) With the G.P. \(1, 2, 4\): products \(2, 12, 72\) (\(r = 6\)); quotients \(2, 3, \frac{9}{2}\) (\(r = \frac{3}{2}\)).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why are they true? In each case work out the ratio of two consecutive new terms:
(i) \(\frac{kg_n}{kg_{n-1}} = r\): the \(k\) cancels, so the ratio is unchanged.
(ii) \(\frac{1/b}{1/a} = \frac{a}{b} = \frac{1}{r}\): the new ratio is \(\frac{1}{r}\).
(iii) \(\frac{b^{n}}{a^{n}} = \left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^{n} = r^{n}\).
(iv) \(\frac{b}{a} = \frac{c}{b}\) (equal ratios) gives \(b^{2} = ac\) on cross-multiplying. Here \(a, b, c\) must be non-zero: \(0, 0, 5\) satisfies \(b^{2} = ac\) but is not a G.P.
(v) \(\log a_n = \log a_1 + (n-1)\log r\), an A.P. with common difference \(\log r\). The numbers must be positive because \(\log\) is defined only for positive numbers.
(vi) The ratios multiply (or divide): \(\frac{a_nb_n}{a_{n-1}b_{n-1}} = r_1r_2\) and the quotients have ratio \(\frac{r_1}{r_2}\).

blocks.title: Example 12
blocks.problem: Find the eighth term of a geometric sequence for which \(a_1 = -3\) and \(r = -2\).
steps:
Given: \(a_1 = -3\), \(r = -2\), \(n = 8\).
To find: \(a_8\).
Method: three of the four quantities in \(a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}\) are known, so substitute directly.

Step 1: Substitute in the general term
\[a_n = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}\]
\[a_8 = (-3) \cdot (-2)^{8-1}\]
Why: the eighth term needs \(r\) multiplied \(8 - 1 = 7\) times.

Step 2: Evaluate the power
\[a_8 = (-3) \cdot (-128)\]
Why: \(2^{7} = 128\), and an odd power of a negative number is negative, so \((-2)^{7} = -128\).

Step 3: Multiply
\[a_8 = 384\]
Why: negative \(\times\) negative = positive; \(3 \times 128 = 384\).

Check:
The terms are \(-3, 6, -12, 24, -48, 96, -192, 384\): the eighth is 384.

blocks.title: Example 13
blocks.problem: Write an equation for the \(n\)th term of the geometric sequence \(3, 12, 48, 192, \ldots\)
steps:
Given: the G.P. \(3, 12, 48, 192, \ldots\)
To find: a formula for \(a_n\).
Method: find \(a_1\) and \(r\), then put them in \(a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}\), leaving \(n\) as a letter.

Step 1: Read \(a_1\) and \(r\)
\[a_1 = 3,\quad r = \dfrac{12}{3} = 4\]
Why: \(r\) is any term divided by its previous term; also \(\frac{48}{12} = \frac{192}{48} = 4\).

Step 2: Write the general term
\[a_n = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1}\]
\[a_n = 3 \cdot 4^{n-1}\]
Why: the question asks for an equation, so \(n\) stays as a variable.

blocks.title: Example 14
blocks.problem: Find the tenth term of a geometric sequence for which \(a_4 = 108\) and \(r = 3\).
steps:
Given: \(a_4 = 108\), \(r = 3\).
To find: \(a_{10}\).
Method: \(a_1\) is not given. Step 1: use \(a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}\) with \(n = 4\) to find \(a_1\). Step 2: use it again with \(n = 10\).

Check:
From \(a_4\) to \(a_{10}\) we multiply by \(r\) six times: \(a_{10} = a_4 \cdot r^{6} = 108 \cdot 729 = 78732\). Same answer.

blocks.title: Example 15
blocks.problem: Find the \(5^{\text{th}}\) term of the G.P., \(3, 6, 12, \ldots\)
steps:
Given: the G.P. \(3, 6, 12, \ldots\)
To find: \(a_5\).
Method: find \(r\) from the given terms, then use \(a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}\) with \(n = 5\).

Step 1: Find \(r\)
Here \(a_1 = 3\), \(a_2 = 6\), \(a_3 = 12\), therefore
\[r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{6}{3} = 2\]
Why: dividing a term by the previous one gives \(r\) (and \(\frac{12}{6} = 2\) agrees).

Check:
Continue doubling: \(3, 6, 12, 24, 48\). The fifth term is 48.

blocks.title: Example 16
steps:
Given: \(a_4 = \frac{8}{27}\), \(a_7 = -\frac{64}{729}\).
To find: \(a_n\) (the general term).
Method: to find \(a_n\) we have to find \(a_1\) and \(r\). Write both given terms with \(a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}\) ...(i); dividing one by the other removes \(a_1\) and gives \(r\).

Step 1: Write the two given terms
\[a_4 = a_1 r^{4-1} = a_1 r^{3}\]
\[a_1 r^{3} = \dfrac{8}{27} \quad \text{(ii)}\]
\[a_7 = a_1 r^{7-1} = a_1 r^{6}\]
\[a_1 r^{6} = \dfrac{-64}{729} \quad \text{(iii)}\]
Why: each given term becomes an equation in the two unknowns \(a_1\) and \(r\).

Step 2: Divide (iii) by (ii)
\[\dfrac{a_7}{a_4} = \dfrac{a_1 r^{6}}{a_1 r^{3}} = r^{3}\]
\[r^{3} = \dfrac{-64/729}{8/27} = \dfrac{-8}{27}\]
\[r^{3} = \left(\dfrac{-2}{3}\right)^{3}\]
\[\Rightarrow r = -\dfrac{2}{3}\]
Why: \(a_1\) cancels in the division. \(\frac{64}{729} \times \frac{27}{8} = \frac{8}{27}\). We take only the real value of \(r\) (the other two cube roots of \(-\frac{8}{27}\) are complex numbers).

Step 3: Find \(a_1\)
Put \(r^{3} = -\frac{8}{27}\) in (ii):
\[a_1\left(-\dfrac{8}{27}\right) = \dfrac{8}{27}\]
\[\Rightarrow a_1 = -1\]
Why: equation (ii) contains \(r^{3}\), which we already know, so no further cubing is needed.

Check:
\(n = 4\): \((-1)^{4}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{3} = \frac{8}{27}\). \(n = 7\): \((-1)^{7}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{6} = -\frac{64}{729}\). Both given terms are reproduced.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Multiplying or dividing every term of a G.P. by the same non-zero number keeps it a G.P. (same \(r\)).
2. Reciprocals of a G.P. form a G.P. (ratio \(\frac{1}{r}\)); powers of a G.P. form a G.P. (ratio \(r^{n}\)).
3. Non-zero \(a, b, c\) are in G.P. exactly when \(b^{2} = ac\).
4. Logs of a G.P. of positive numbers form an A.P.
5. Term-by-term products and quotients of two G.Ps. are G.Ps.
6. When two terms are given, divide them: \(a_1\) cancels and a power of \(r\) remains (Example 16).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \((-2)^{7} = 128\): an odd power of a negative number is negative.
2. In Example 16, taking \(r = \frac{2}{3}\): the cube root of a negative number is negative.
3. Using \(b^{2} = ac\) when a term is zero: G.P. terms are never zero.
4. Thinking that adding the same number to every term keeps a G.P.: \(2, 6, 18\) plus 1 gives \(3, 7, 19\), not a G.P. Only multiplying or dividing works.
